entities.name: Bentivenga da Bentivengi
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Bentivenga dei Bentivenghi, a prominent Italian Franciscan friar, rose to the cardinalate in 1278, playing a crucial role in the administration of the Roman Curia and the spiritual governance of the nascent Franciscan Order during a period of significant papal centralization and intellectual ferment in the late 13th century. His career, spanning the pontificates of Nicholas III, Martin IV, and Honorius IV, epitomized the integration of mendicant orders into the highest echelons of the Church, influencing canon law, monastic discipline, and diplomatic relations across Latin Christendom. Born in Acquasparta, Umbria, his influence extended far beyond his native Italy, touching upon theological debates and the emerging university system.

Elevated to Cardinal-Bishop of Albano by Pope Nicholas III on March 12, 1278, Bentivenga quickly became a trusted advisor and a key figure in the papal chancellery. He served as Penitentiary Major from 1279 until his death, overseeing the complex system of papal dispensations, absolutions, and spiritual judgments. His work involved intricate legal interpretations and pastoral care, directly impacting countless individuals and ecclesiastical bodies. Furthermore, he participated in the conclave of 1280-1281 that elected Martin IV and the conclave of 1285 that elected Honorius IV, demonstrating his consistent presence and influence in papal succession.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Bentivenga da Bentivengi's career as a cardinal and Penitentiary Major significantly contributed to the administrative and judicial centralization of the medieval papacy, leaving a lasting impact on canon law and curial governance. His role also exemplifies the integration and influence of mendicant orders within the Church's highest echelons.
